Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers

Nepal-Tibet floods – latest updates

Visual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfolded

Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating ​floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.

Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.

In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues .

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”

She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.

“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China , posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.

The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the ​immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.

Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminisging that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.

Shah said the ​catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

stories.title: Trump tells FCC to punish journalist for calling his election results "mixed"
stories.summary: Trump furious at NBC's Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump furious at NBC’s Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.

President Trump yesterday demanded that the Federal Communications Commission punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements. In the latest example of how Trump is using the FCC to harass reporters and news organizations that he dislikes, he said Meet the Press host Kristen Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” for what he claimed was a “purposeful inaccuracy.”

“Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm. How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post .

A separate post from Trump yesterday said, “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” Trump also posted a rant on Friday about New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her “an unattractive person both inside and out” who “should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.” Trump referred to Haberman throughout his post as “Maggot Haberman.”

Trump’s post about Welker included an image purporting to show he has near-perfect results in his endorsements this year. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.

Perhaps indicating that he will refer additional journalists for FCC punishment, Trump wrote that Welker “is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”

Trump’s FCC chair has eagerly obeyed orders

The idea of the FCC punishing reporters for basic analysis of election results would have seemed far-fetched in previous administrations. The FCC website says the commission “cannot prevent the broadcast of any particular point of view,” and that it “generally will not intervene” in complaints about “one-sided news reports” because “it would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.”

Even during Trump’s first term, then-FCC Chairman Ajit Pai said that under the First Amendment, “the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast.” Pai made the comment less than a week after Trump called on the FCC to revoke broadcast licenses from NBC and other networks for “fake news.”

An FCC investigation of Welker over an ordinary statement about election results seems much less far-fetched under Carr, who has embraced his role as Trump’s chief censor. Carr has made it clear he takes orders from Trump , abandoning his previous position—which he held under Democratic presidents —that the FCC must operate independently of White House interference.

Welker said in an appearance on NBC 4 Washington that Trump “has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries” and that “he’s had some mixed results but most recently his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course the sister of the late Senator Lindsay Graham, was successful in her primary battle.” Trump’s post attacking Welker claimed that “the story of [Graham’s] Victory was hardly covered by anybody,” despite Welker mentioning it in the very statement that triggered Trump’s wrath.

Poynter Senior Media Writer Tom Jones writes , “What Welker said about Trump’s endorsements having mixed results was true. Trump just didn’t like it.” While Trump praised himself for his successful endorsements, he didn’t mention primary losses by Republican gubernatorial candidates Burt Jones in Georgia and Randy Feenstra in Iowa and the failed re-election bid by Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida).

Carr uses news-distortion policy to threaten networks

An NBC News spokesperson told several media outlets that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.” We contacted NBC News and will update this article if it has any further comment.

Welker is hardly the first TV journalist to discuss Trump’s mixed endorsement results. “Already, just this month alone, six of the president’s endorsed candidates have lost their races, and so there are questions about the power of his endorsements,” CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene said on Inside Politics .

In June, Trump abruptly ended an interview with Welker after she challenged his claims of election rigging in California. Trump stated that “all I have to do is look” when Welker asked him for evidence of cheating. “That’s not evidence,” Welker responded.

If Carr does investigate Welker, he could do so under the FCC’s news distortion policy. Carr has repeatedly invoked the rarely enforced news distortion policy and a rule against broadcast hoaxes in various threats to Trump’s perceived enemies in the media. We asked the FCC chairman’s office today if the commission will investigate Welker and will update this article if we get a response.

Previous FCC leaders set such a high bar for proving news distortion that the policy was all but abandoned until Carr made it a focal point of his attempts to punish broadcasters. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for news distortion if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel’s show.

Trump and FCC try to reshape the media

While Carr can cause trouble for licensed broadcasters and networks simply by issuing threats, he went far beyond mere threats in the case of ABC. The Carr FCC ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates and justified the proceeding by accusing ABC of violating anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices.

ABC owner Disney is fighting back with a lawsuit against Carr and the FCC , saying it has faced a campaign of censorship in retaliation for the protected speech of its journalists and network programs. Both conservative and liberal groups have urged the FCC to back off.

The Trump administration has also sought to reshape the media through merger approvals. Paramount won FCC approval to buy Skydance after agreeing to install what Carr called a “bias monitor” at CBS. Paramount later won Justice Department approval to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, months after CEO David Ellison reportedly told Trump administration officials that he would make big changes at the Warner-owned CNN.

In March, Trump and Carr demanded more positive media coverage of the Iran war, with Carr claiming without evidence that broadcasters aired “hoaxes and news distortions.” Last year, Carr accused Comcast of news distortion when its subsidiary NBC refused to adopt the Trump administration narrative on the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, responded to Trump’s latest threat yesterday. “As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote . “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

stories.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
stories.summary: The governor of the Bank of England warned of AI's “volatility” caused by energy shocks from the US-Iran war.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 31 August 2026

The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms , including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes as the UK government is seeking to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

Andrew Bailey wants those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release"

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

The FSB which Bailey leads is a global watchdog which monitors finance ministry officials, banks and securities regulators. It includes officials from the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Japan, Australia, China and Saudi Arabia.

stories.body:
Starmer to quit parliament, triggering byelection in Holborn and St Pancras in north London

Keir Starmer is going to resign as an MP, his local paper, the Camden New Journal, is reporting.

When he resigned as PM, Starmer said he planned to stay as a backbench MP until the next election. But he has changed his mind, the paper reports. It says:

double quotation mark After weeks of speculation about his future plans, [Starmer] chose his local newspaper to explain why he felt it was the “right time” to leave the House of Commons and concentrate on new work on international affairs. He told the New Journal that, after leaving Downing Street at the end of July, he had reflected on what lay ahead and that he was ready to “pass the baton to a successor”, adding: “It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country and to have taken over from Frank Dobson, who was such a great constituency MP and a member of the last Labour government. I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world. “I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. It’s work I started before I became an MP and it’s work I’m keen to continue after I’m an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other.”

This means there will be a byelection in Holborn and St Pancras in north London, where Starmer had a majority of 11,572 at the last election. At one point there were fears this could lead to Labour losing the seat to the Green party, but in recent weeks Labour’s national poll ratings have been rising and support for the Greens is on the wane.

How Zack Polanski told an interviewer in April he would 'almost certainly' stand in any London byelection

In an interview in April, Zack Polanski , the Green party leader, said he would “almost certainly” run in a future byelection in London. He told La Repubblica’s Antonello Guerrera:

double quotation mark So when Gorton and Denton came up and people asked me, obsessively, are you going to run? And I didn’t run because, although I’m from Manchester, I’ve lived in London nearly 20, or over 20, years now. And so there would have been a narrative to say, oh, it’s my hometown, I’m going back. But I think that would have been dishonest. Secondly, I knew we had amazing candidates like Hannah Spencer, where I wanted a candidate from a local community. I think I was proven to be right. If there was another byelection outside of London, I still wouldn’t be running in it. We have amazing candidates right across the rest of the country. If there’s a byelection in London, I’ll almost certainly be running, well, depending on where it is. I live in Hackney, so if it’s somewhere around Hackney, so you could be looking to Hackney North, Hackney South, Walthamstow, Holborn and St Pancras, if Keir Starmer is going anywhere, and even, you know, Tower Hamlets. I think, generally, around the east of London, in the northeast, I’ve lived there for a long time. I have a connection to the place. I think there are other places in London where I’m already a London Assembly member, but I have less legitimate connection.

Keir Starmer has posed a statement on social media about his decision to stand down as an MP. It is much the same as what he told the Camden New Journal. (See 1.06pm .)

Is it unusual for a former PM to quit the Commons before a general election?

Keir Starmer is not the first ex-PM to change his mind about remaining in the House of Commons until the next election as a backbencher. David Cameron also resigned as PM in July, only to quit the Commons for good two months later. He initially thought he could stay as MP without causing trouble for his successor, Theresa May, but quickly realised on some issues he would not be able to support her. (He announced he was going very soon after she hinted she would lift his block on new grammar schools.)

Tony Blair did not even leave it that long; he resigned as an MP the same day he left Downing Street, realising that if he were to stay in the Commons with Gordon Brown as PM, that would probably be intolerable for both of them.

Boris Johnson also resigned early as an MP after leaving Downing Street – but that was because the privileges committee was about to say he should be suspended for lying about Partygate.

Other ex-PMs, like Theresa May and Liz Truss, have remained in the Commons after being forced out of No 10 midway through a parliament. May even stood for re-election at the subsequent general election (2019) following her return to the backbenches, as did Harold Wilson (in 1979).

Most PMs who lose office at a general election when their party loses only subsequently serve one more term in the Commons as a backbencher. But James Callaghan served for two more parliaments after he lost the 1979 general election, ending up as father of the house, and Edward Heath spent another 27 years in the Commons after losing both 1974 general elections.

Before the 2024 election critics claimed that, if Rishi Sunak lost, he would swiftly give up his seat and move to California. But he remains MP for Richmond and North Allerton and seems determined to stay until the next election.

Andy Burnham will start his Commons statement at 3.30pm. The Commons authorities have confirmed that there will be no urgent questions (which would have come first).

The statement is being described as being about “government direction”.

Afterwards, from about 5.30pm, Alex Norris, the justice secretary, will give one on the prisoner early release scheme. And then Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will give a statement on policing in Cleveland.

Starmer leaves 'shameful legacy', says Your Party

Your Party , the leftwing party founded by Jeremy Corbyn and others, has said Keir Starmer leaves a “shameful legacy”. A Your Party spokesperson said:

double quotation mark Keir Starmer leaves behind a party hollowed out, millions of voters disillusioned and a shameful record of British complicity in the genocide in Gaza. He entered politics as a human rights lawyer and leaves having abandoned those principles when they mattered most. Now he is abandoning his constituents too. That’s certainly a legacy! Starmer may run, but he can’t hide from the shameful legacy he leaves behind.

Corbyn was suspended and then ultimately expelled from Labour after Starmer replaced him as the party’s leader.

Burnham says government has had 'strong sense of momentum' since he became PM

Andy Burnham told colleagues at cabinet that he thought the government had established “a strong sense of momentum” since he became PM.

At the No 10 lobby briefing, giving a readout from what was said at cabinet, the PM’s spokesperson said:

double quotation mark The prime minister opened cabinet by thanking colleagues for establishing a strong sense of momentum in his first weeks in office. He said the country had noticed a change of pace, with the government setting the agenda and starting the process of giving local areas the levers they need to create good growth. He said that during his summer tour it was clear that life was hard for many people, but that they wanted to have hope and hear a positive outlook for the country.

According to the spokesperson, Burnham also used his opening remarks to thank Alex Norris, the justice secretary, for his work on changing the prisoner early release scheme and Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, for her “relentless work on small boat crossings”. (See 9.29am .)

Starmer says it is 'right to step down' given his decision to focus now on international affairs

Here are some more quotes from the interview Keir Starme r gave to the Camden New Journal announcing his decision to stand down.

Starmer said he wanted to focus on issues like international affairs, defence, security, trade and technology. He said:

double quotation mark I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world. I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. It’s work I started before I became an MP and it’s work I’m keen to continue after I’m an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other.

He said that, given his new priorities, he thought it was right to leave parliament. He said:

double quotation mark I think once you’ve been prime minister, it’s important to answer the question: what are you going to do next? Having decided I’m going to concentrate on international affairs, I think it’s right to step down [as MP].

He said he would not be backing any candidate seeking the Labour nomination to succeed him. He said:

double quotation mark The constituency Labour party has got many, many fantastic people and there will be no shortage of first class candidates.

He highlighted changes the Labour government had made to his constituency. He said:

double quotation mark In terms of some of the things that have changed: we are opening ten breakfast clubs across the constituency – five of them opened in April, five more will be opened when the schools go back this week. I think breakfast clubs make a huge difference for children and parents because everybody knows that a child that hasn’t eaten before they try to start learning is not going to learn as well as other children.” Free school meals are coming again this week, that’s 4,600 children in the constituency that will now benefit, the minimum wage increase will make a difference to thousands of workers across Camden who are on or near the minimum wage and there’s an increase in the number of GPs. The two child benefit cap being lifted will affect 2,500 children in the constituency who will now begin to be lifted out of poverty. Then there’s the Renters’ Rights Act – 16,500 renters in Holborn and St Pancras – and of course everybody who is at work will benefit under the Employment Rights Act.

And he said no Labour leader had ever achieved what he did in rescuing the party from defeat. He said:

double quotation mark My years on the frontline were basically six and a half years because it was from picking up the Labour party in 2019 from the worst election result since 1935 and turning it around to a general election landslide victory in 2024, while most people said it wouldn’t be possible to win the election in 2024 – let alone win it with a landslide. No leader has ever pulled such a swing across from such a low base to a landslide in the way that we did.

Greens don't rule out Zack Polanski standing in Holborn and St Pancras byelection

The Greens have not ruled out Zack Polanski, the party’s leader, standing as their candidate to replace Keir Starmer as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, my colleague Jessica Elgot reports .

double quotation mark NEW - A Green party spokesman said: “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years.” Sounds like Polanski might fancy a tilt at Holborn and St Pancras.

Tories describe Starmer's decision to trigger 'costly' byelection as 'yet another U-turn' given pledge to stay as backbencher

This is from Kevin Hollinrake , the Conservative party chair, on Keir Starmer resigning as an MP.

double quotation mark Whilst we have disagreed with almost all of Sir Keir Starmer’s decisions, I wish him and his family well for the future. It is fitting that his final act as a member of parliament is yet another U-turn having pledged to stay on. The decision to stand down will mean a costly byelection for taxpayers at a time when Andy Burnham are John Healey are plotting tax rises on hardworking families across the country. The Conservatives look forward to giving the people of Holborn and St Pancras a chance to vote for a stronger economy and a stronger country in the weeks ahead.

stories.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
stories.summary: The move will trigger a by-election to replace the former prime minister in his London constituency.

stories.body:
Since he resigned as prime minister in July, there was speculation over whether Sir Keir would stay on as MP

Published 1 September 2026, 12:21 BST

Former Prime Pinister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham makes his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Announcing his resignation, he told the Camden New Journal , external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He added: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

'Another U-turn'

Sir Keir's announcement comes hours before Burnham is due to deliver his first statement in the Commons as prime minister , setting out his priorities and taking questions from MPs.

Conservative chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".

A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat.

Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.

Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.

Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.

Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.

A spokesperson for the party said Polanksi, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

Starmer: What Went Wrong?

From triumph to turmoil, the story of how Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership unravelled, from Labour’s historic 2024 landslide to the fatal miscalculations and internal revolt that forced him from power.

Previous PMs

While it is unclear exactly what type of international affairs role Sir Keir may take up, global issues and diplomacy dominated his time as PM.

stories.title: Meta accepts U.S. safety rules while pitching softer tools abroad
stories.summary: As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech Giants

As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.

In June, Indian actor Hiten Tejwani told his 732,000 followers that “Instagram is okay” in a reel promoting Meta’s Teen Accounts. Ironically, Tejwani had barred his 17-year-old twin son and daughter from using social media until they turned 16.

The reel was made after a Zoom call with Meta representatives, who explained what their campaign endorsed. Teen Accounts, launched in 2024, gives 13- to 16-year-olds private accounts, screen-time limits, and age-appropriate content. Tejwani, who was paid for the campaign but did not disclose the amount, told Rest of World that he agreed to participate because he saw it as an effort to inform parents rather than encourage every child to join social media.

There has been a global rise in the number of such reels in recent months, as Meta pursues influencer campaigns promoting Teen Accounts, particularly in countries that are mulling a social media ban for children under 16, according to a recent report by Tech Transparency Project, a Washington-based research organization.

Meta is using parent influencers to both soften its image and fight back against the existential threat of social media bans for kids under 16, Katie Paul, director of Tech Transparency Project, told Rest of World .

The campaign comes at a time when Meta is facing heat in the U.S. over child safety concerns. On August 26, the company settled a major trial in the U.S., agreeing to make several safety limitations the default option for teens. Australia, Brazil, and Indonesia have already banned social media for kids under 16. At least 22 other countries are reportedly designing and proposing similar policies .

“If countries around the world follow the lead of Australia and enact these bans, Meta will be cut off from young people who are essential to its growth plans,” Paul said.

Meta’s campaign against social media restrictions

Tech Transparency Project found that Meta has been pushing a narrative of safety through “momfluencers” across the world, from India to Canada to Indonesia.

While the campaign plays out slightly differently in each country, the fundamental strategy is this: Meta pays Instagram influencer parents or celebrities with large followings — and in some cases, child safety groups — to promote Teen Accounts, Paul said. A teen account on Facebook or Instagram allows parents to supervise content and communication for under-16s.

“The underlying message is that Meta is capable of self-regulating child safety protection and that bans are unnecessary,” Paul said. “Some of these influencers have hundreds of thousands and even millions of followers, making them a potent tool for Meta’s corporate messaging.”

Meta has also hosted several “screen smart” events across the world, including in the U.S., New Zealand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, to promote teen safety and parental supervision. In Australia, it sponsored a youth mental health service conducting “ safety camps .” In Indonesia, Meta commissioned a survey , which revealed “overwhelming” parental support for teen accounts with safety features.

Influencing controls

Age verification tools are less than ideal, but they’re still better than outright bans, David Greene, senior counsel at nonprofit digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Rest of World .

“Mandated age limits are designed to deny young people their fundamental human rights — to access information, arts, and culture, to form communities, to speak, and to play,” Greene said. “Age estimation technology threatens all users’ privacy by collecting people’s sensitive, personal information, exposing them to risk of data breaches and government data demands, and chilling speech on sensitive issues.”

Parental tools and youth accounts are a better option than bans, he said. There is probably a role for broader-based social media literacy education as well, “whether that happens through influencers, the government, parents, or peers.”

Snehaalata Shah, an Indian parenting and travel blogger, was approached by an agency for the Teen Accounts campaign. She did not wish to disclose the name of the agency. This was her first paid campaign for Meta.

“They gave us a brief idea where I have to inculcate the teen account features in the middle of the script,” she told Rest of World . “I made a script, and a little bit of changes were done by the agency.” The teen account for her 14-year-old daughter lets Shah keep track of follow and direct message requests and screen time.

“The main takeaway for parents is that there are tools and safeguards available to make social media more age-appropriate for teenagers and to give parents more control and reassurance,” Sonam Jaggi, who runs the account @momavengers with 322,000 followers, told Rest of World . The promo shot by the mom of two kids — 8 and 1 — has amassed 310 million views , and more than half a million likes.

A November 2025 report by a Meta whistleblower and several online kids safety organizations evaluated 47 out of 53 safety features for teens. It found that 64% of the features were broken, missing, or ineffective.

Shah posted a promo reel for Teen Accounts for her 238,000 followers on July 7 — coincidentally the same day Meta published a statement claiming it had “ zero-tolerance ” for child sexual abuse material, and that it had taken down more than 160,000 accounts.

“If every country bans Instagram or Facebook under 16, of course, there would be loss to [Meta],” Shah told Rest of World. She said she recognized there may be a business motive driving these ads. But given that her 6-year-old son knows how to switch accounts on YouTube instead of logging off when the child time restriction notification pops up, she would still promote the tools to protect her teen.

Tejwani, too, is standing by his decision, but as a parent. Although it was a paid campaign to begin with, his heart is in it, and he’s still happy to entertain questions from other parents and media.

“It is compensation we have to charge, definitely. But otherwise, if I’m talking about it right now, if somebody’s asking me otherwise, this is not a paid thing. I will definitely inform everyone,” Tejwani told Rest of World .

India’s data center boom is leaving the people it displaces with nothing

Communities are being left behind as AI companies secure tax breaks, cheap land from willing governments.

America’s immigration policy is driving away future AI leaders

Visa restrictions are deterring international AI talent from building companies in the U.S., giving other nations including China an opportunity to catch up.

The UAE is fighting AI hackers with AI of its own

Attacks on the country’s banks, aviation, and energy systems have climbed since the war with Iran began. Its answer is a homegrown AI security industry.

A.B. 1709 is a massive privacy and free speech nightmare. Denying young people access to digital forums (or stripping out the basic tools needed to navigate them) does nothing to make young people safer or healthier. Research shows that social media bans are ineffectual , and can be harmful when they deny young people opportunities to develop their own voices and perspectives, whether that means sharing art, practicing religion, or engaging in politics.

Far from protecting children, the bill will also severely restrict access to constitutionally protected speech and push platforms to implement invasive age-verification methods, such as requiring government IDs or biometric scanning. Age-gating requirements will force everyone to give big tech companies even more personal information . To verify who can pass through online gates, companies will collect even more data, concentrating power in corporate hands rather than protecting users. This creates massive honeypots of sensitive personal data , severely damages online anonymity , and exposes users of all ages to heightened data breach risks .

Finally, A.B. 1709 introduces legal confusion by creating provisions that conflict with already enacted legislation like A.B. 1043 and S.B. 976 . Rather than offering regulatory clarity on already-passed laws, California will only end up spending valuable resources to defend a law bound to be tied up in court.

stories.body:
Warning signs visible days before Nepal glacier collapse, report suggests

Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency .

The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.

Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.

The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings . Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.

The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.

“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.

“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”

It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of ​the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.

As police in Kathmandu buried dozens of bodies in multiple trenches, Nepal’s disaster agency said that 1,003 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreign nationals.

The 1,003 figure given here is seven lower than the death toll provided by Nepal’s foreign ministry spokesperson earlier today (see this post ).

In its latest update, China reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including 261 foreigners.

In the capital Kathmandu , crowds lined up to search for their missing relatives, posting photographs on a long wall outside a hospital in the fading hope of finding them alive.

Debu Sapkota, a 58-year-old driver, came to post photos of his 83-year-old mother-in-law and her granddaughter who went missing in the town of Trishuli Bazaar after being swept away by last week’s surge.

A warning alert sounded, but the elderly woman was “too old to run”, he told AP. “Her granddaughter was helping her escape, but both were swept away.”

Sapkota said he no longer has “any hope that they survived”, after witnesses saw them being carried away by the torrent.

“I am here hoping to find their bodies,” he said, holding up photos of the two missing women dressed in traditional clothes.

Here is footage filmed using a drone in the village of Devighat , Nepal , that shows damaged houses and shops, while roads remain covered in thick mud.

Local people have been using heavy machinery to clear the debris-covered streets and rescue efforts are continuing across the country.

“No siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds,” says Prof Anjal Prakash, from Flame University in India. He blames a lack of political will to fight the climate crisis and to plan infrastructure for the devastating flood in Nepal and Tibet .

Prof Prakash said:

double quotation mark Nepal’s mountains have been sending warnings for a decade : thinning glaciers, retreating snowlines, permafrost turning to slush under roads and hydropower plants we kept building anyway . We didn’t lack the science, as researchers have tracked this decline for 50 years. We lacked the political will to act on it . Early warning systems are being sold as the fix, but no siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds . The real failure sits upstream, in land-use decisions that pushed settlements and infrastructure onto riverbanks our ancestors deliberately avoided, and in a global economy still burning the fossil fuels that are cooking these glaciers from the inside out . Every villager who watched that valley disappear paid for emissions decisions made thousands of kilometres away . Until governments treat the Himalayas as a climate frontline rather than a postcard backdrop, Rasuwa won’t be the last name we’re forced to memorise .

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said:

double quotation mark For years, scientists and local communities have been warning that the Hindu Kush Himalayas are at huge risk from climate change. We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe , with vulnerable communities often hardest hit. But the solutions to global heating are equally clear – especially a faster global shift from fossil fuels to renewables and more investment in climate resilience.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues .

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” You can read more here:

Nepal last week turned down foreign ​involvement in general search and rescue but said it needed specialised services and advanced technological support in areas such as life-detecting machines, large refrigerators and pre-fabricated bridges.

Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country and Nepal is now working with experts from other countries to help with rescue operations.

But the apparent hesitance to accept immediate foreign help has come under scrutiny as the damage and scale of the disaster increasingly comes into view.

Speaking to NPR , Bhim Gautam, chief executive officer of the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal, said his country lacks “technology, equipment and expertise” to carry out effective rescue operations at hydropower projects.

“Our expertise is only in dealing with small flooding. We have never faced a situation like this before,” Gautam told the outlet, adding that his industry’s leaders had to “pressure the government” to allow in foreign rescue workers, a claim that we have not been able to independently verify.

“Late last week, the government approved rescue teams from China , India and Australia to come,” Gautam said. “But it is so late now.”

Death toll from floods rises to 1,010, with thousands still missing, Nepal's foreign ministry says

Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, has been holding a press briefing on the floods, providing updates on the search efforts and scale of the disaster. Here are some of the main points from what he said:

The national priority is to save lives, locate the missing, rescue survivors and provide urgent relief to those affected.

More than 21,000 personnel from Nepal’s army, police and armed police forces are engaged in search and rescue, relief and evacuation operations while the government coordinates with its neighbours and the international community, which is providing vital equipment and expertise.

1,010 bodies have been recovered, about 4,000 people are missing and more than 11,800 people have been rescued, including about 324 foreign nationals.

Approximately 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain missing – these figures continue to be updated.

Specialised tunnel rescue teams are working to find those feared to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River including at the Chilime, Langtang and Upper Trishuli 3A sites.

Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah said that the disaster highlighted the need for action to combat the climate crisis.

“This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change,” Shah said in a social media post on Monday night.

“Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community.”

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China’s second batch of relief supplies for Nepal was expected to ship today, including drones, DNA testing and water purification equipment.

Chinese DNA testing experts will also help Nepal identity bodies, he said. Beijing has said it will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

43,000 women and girls in Nepal need urgent humanitarian assistance, UN warns

An estimated 43,000 women and girls in Nepal are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance following the flood disaster last week, according to Christine Arab, UN Women regional director for Asia and the Pacific, who has been at a press briefing in Geneva.

Arab said women are running out of food, and safe water to drink, while facing exclusion from decisions that will shape their recovery even though they are likely to pick up more unpaid care work in the home.

She also highlighted how disasters increase the risk of trafficking, exploitation and gender-based violence while shrinking the availability of protection services for the most vulnerable.

“When there are no separate or safe latrines, adequate lighting or privacy, women and girls can face risks simply when using the toilet, bathing, sleeping, or moving around after dark,” Arab said.

“Women in the worst-affected areas tell us that food is their most urgent priority right now. Before the floods, women in Nepal were more likely to eat least and to eat last in their families, with serious consequences for their own health, particularly those who are pregnant or breastfeeding,” she added.

Warning signs visible days before Nepal glacier collapse, report suggests

Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency .

The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.

Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.

The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings . Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.

The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.

“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.

“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”

It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of ​the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.

At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities.

Emergency crews are using aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.

Nepal tourism department publishes list of names of missing people

Nepal’s tourism department published a list of the names of the people still missing, as of Sunday evening, after the catastrophic flooding in the district of Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit provinces in Nepal. It said there were 164 people from Nepal that remain unaccounted for and 25 from China.

It said a total of 583 foreigners were missing, with the highest number from India ( 183 ), followed by the US ( 64 ) and then Malaysia ( 55 ). There are 33 people from the UK that have been identified as missing.

Beijing’s state media reports that 16 people died in Tibet, with 546 missing, but advocacy groups have accused China of heavily underreporting the death toll from flooding in border regions with Nepal, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.

The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions .

The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state-run CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.

You can read more in this story by my colleagues, Cait Kelly and William Christou , here:

Death toll from Nepal-China flood disaster exceeds 1,000, authorities say

The death toll from the catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has passed 1,000 as of Tuesday morning, officials said, with authorities reportedly burying hundreds of unidentified victims after the flood disaster overwhelmed morgues.

Nepal’s disaster agency said in an update on Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners .

Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing.

The initial 72 hours after a disaster are viewed as critical to a rescue operation and there are fading hopes that the missing will be found alive.

Rescue efforts nonetheless persist, but have been complicated by challenging terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather.

The devastating floods occurred last Wednesday when a huge section of a glacier in the Himalayas came loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive wall of water and mud that rushed down rivers and valleys.

The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed vital infrastructure such as power stations, roads and bridges.

Much of the rescue efforts are now focused on trying to reach the 900 or so missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal.

“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the Reuters news agency on Monday.

About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing, as my colleague notes in this story .

Many people are feared to still be trapped in the sprawling network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River, which flows through central Nepal.

stories.summary: The UK says Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

Published 34 minutes ago

Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported , external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine soldiers.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.

The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

Defence spending pledges

Reports of this proposal have re-emerged in recent days in relation to defence spending.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will honour a commitment made by predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to devote 3.5% of UK gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence spending by 2035.

On Tuesday, Chancellor John Healey told The Times , external he would "set out a clear path" to meeting that Nato pledge at the next government spending review, expected in the spring of next year.

He added that this would also include a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP.

Healey resigned as defence secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government following a row over military spending.

His resignation letter in June expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to hit the 3% spending target, which he believed should happen by 2030.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The CDC has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer.

The Trump administration is halting vital federal research on the foodborne parasite Cyclospora, despite the record-breaking, nationwide outbreak of the diarrheal pathogen, according to Politico .

Of the three research programs that represent nearly all of the Cyclospora work at the US Department of Agriculture, two have been defunded, and the third is about to lose every scientist working on it. The Trump administration is shuttering the USDA’s Beltsville Agricultural Research Center near Washington, DC, and moving its work to a location in Iowa. That includes relocating the remaining Cyclospora research.

Although the research is still funded, insiders told Politico that not one of the scientists working on the project plans to relocate from Maryland to Iowa. Instead, they are either retiring, being reassigned to a different project, or leaving the USDA’s research services.

“They will have no parasitologists,” one USDA employee told Politico. “There will be a big knowledge gap.”

The US is experiencing the largest Cyclospora outbreak ever recorded. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has tallied nearly 30,000 confirmed and probable cases this summer. At least 922 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, and two have died. Since 2018, the US has generally reported between 2,000 and 5,000 cases, though the US reported 1,180 cases in 2025.

Lost research opportunities

Cyclospora is difficult to work with in a laboratory compared to other foodborne pathogens, such as E. coli or Salmonella. Cyclospora grow and reproduce only in the human gut, not in lab conditions. Although the parasite can be isolated from feces in labs, it can sometimes be difficult to fish out; it can be shed intermittently or at low levels, requiring repeat fecal samples from an infected person. The parasite is also harder to study using genetic techniques. It has a much larger genome than bacteria, making genomic sequencing costlier and more laborious. It also reproduces sexually, meaning each generation will have new mixes of genes, making it harder to trace back lineages of the parasite to a single contaminated food. That’s in contrast to bacteria, which reproduce asexually, creating clones that are often nearly identical and easy to trace.

With this year’s outbreak, researchers hoped for a surge in understanding of the parasite. “We see this as an enormous opportunity, this current outbreak, to have really a lot of samples that could help us understand these outbreaks better,” another USDA employee told Politico. However, people who worked on the defunded Cyclospora programs are barred from doing any more research and are simply preserving samples they already had from previous outbreaks.

While funding may be restored at a later time, experts said the disruption to the research will be difficult to overcome. “The bigger impact is that there are very few people in the world that study these [parasites],” Joelle Mosso, associate vice president for science growers at the Western Growers Association, a trade group representing produce farmers, told Politico. “It’s not just replacing the lab. It takes decades to build expertise.”

stories.title: EFF to Courts: Don’t Rewrite Copyright Over AI Hype
stories.summary: The history of technology is rife with copyright panics. In the 1980s, major rightsholders ran to Congress and the courts, claiming that videotape recorders (VTR) were “to the American film producer and the American public as the Boston strangler is to the woman home alone .” Then, the Supreme Court declined to embrace the hype, noting that the VTR was capable of all kinds of non-infringing uses, like time-shifting and cautioning courts to avoid rewriting copyright law in response to new technologies. We believe that courts now should be similarly wary about the hype surrounding AI. Hollywood’s hyperbole has echoed that of composer John Phillip Sousa , who claimed in 1906 that the player piano and the gramophone would destroy music composition; portrait artists who feared the camera would replace the paintbrush. None of these things happened. Cameras, for example, sparked a resurgence of portraiture and, by making it possible for more people to create images, led to unexpected developments—like the rise of photojournalism. New markets, new ideas, and new creators are actually what copyright is supposed to promote, not restrict. Using copyright to lock in existing gatekeepers and massive rightsholders’ profits helps neither the public nor individual artists. Generative AI has sparked the latest wave of anxiety and with it a massive wave of litigation. In multiple cases around the U.S. and the world, rightsholders are asking courts to do precisely what the Supreme Court warned against: dramatically expand copyright protections based in substantial part on hyperbole and speculation. They should decline to do so. Copyright owners claim that unless courts abandon 300-year-old copyright principles—and give rightsholders the power to control non-infringing works created by others—an imagined flood of AI-generated works will devastate creative markets. Under this “market dilution” theory, building generative AI tools cannot be fair use because those tools might be encourage the proliferation of competing works. As EFF has explained to the courts in multiple amicus briefs in Concord Music Group, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC and In re Mosaic LLM Litigation , that’s not how copyright works. In-store inflation rises to an annual 1.5% in August, according to a survey for the British Retail Consortium

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a trade body index shows, with higher energy costs pushing up the price of food and AI chip demand making technology more expensive .

In-store inflation stepped up to 1.5% year on year in August, up from 0.9% in July, led by prices for tinned and packaged food which increased by 2.5% against 1.1% in the prior month, according to data from the research company NIQ for the British Retail Consortium.

Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%, amid pressure on growers from the hot dry summer plus hefty fuel and energy costs. However, that marked a slight easing off from the 3.1% recorded in July,

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the consortium, said: “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed.

“In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage. Meanwhile, retailers kept clothing prices low to offer value for families getting ready for the new school year.

“The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.”

Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills.

However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.”

The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields.

Cereals including wheat and barley were hit particularly badly, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006.

Wider consumer price inflation across the UK rose to 2.9% in July with the Iran war affecting energy prices, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics . The agency said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by more costly gas and electricity.

Despite government measures to ease electricity costs, households in Great Britain face the sharpest summer increase in energy bills in four years.

stories.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
stories.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Brands like Uniqlo and Muji have rapidly expanded in India

Published 31 August 2026

India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.

If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.

Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.

Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson , external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.

It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.

MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.

Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.

Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.

More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report , external . GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.

"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC.

Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments in India through some 120 agreements during PM Sanae Takaichi's visit in July

At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.

"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."

Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.

Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.

After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.

But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.

At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.

Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.

Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.

The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently , external , is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".

But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.

India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.

"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."

India's consumer market is growing fast as discretionary incomes rise

For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.

India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.

But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.

"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll , external .

"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."

Also, India remains a tough country to do business.

Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.

An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed , external .

Chinese state media , external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.

It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.
